s10.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:14 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY
body: The only light in the lobby is coming out of the Fishbowl. Somebody has left CNN on in there with the sound off, and the blue of it fills the glass box and spills out through the wall onto the linoleum as far as the mailboxes, and the rest of the lobby is the exit signs and the rain going down the big front windows in sheets.

He hasn’t slept. He got off at one with his hands pruned from the Hobart and lay in the dark in 412 with the rain on the window, and every time he got near sleep he was back in a basement saying it out loud. At ten past three he gave it up and came down in the Carhartt and his sneakers with no socks, with four quarters in his fist for a Coke. The east stairs were wet all the way down from everybody’s shoes. On the lobby bulletin board somebody has pinned a new flyer over the Haiti one, TORNADO??? in marker and a phone number for a guy on Trigo who lost his carport and wants to know if anyone has pictures, and under the front doors the rain has come in a dark tongue across the mat.
Marcus is asleep at the front desk with his cheek on a chemistry textbook, a page of hexagons under his ear and the highlighter still uncapped in his hand.
Lena is in the Fishbowl.

She’s by herself on the couch nearest the set, with her knees drawn up under the gray cardigan and her phone shut in her lap, and the screen is all over her: blue on her face, blue on her hands, blue in the rain still on the window behind her. Across the bottom of the picture the red band says BREAKING — STRONG AFTERSHOCK HITS HAITI — 6.1, and above it, without any sound, a man in a suit is talking to a map.
She hasn’t seen him. He’s standing in the dark of the lobby twenty feet from the glass with the quarters going warm in his hand.

choices.key: At three in the morning you went into the Fishbowl and sat with Lena and the earthquake.
response: He puts the quarters in his pocket and crosses the linoleum, past Marcus and his hexagons, and pulls the glass door. It sticks at the bottom. She hears it, and doesn’t turn her head.

choices.key: At three in the morning you stood at the Fishbowl glass. Lena turned the news off and sat in the dark.
response: He goes as far as the glass and stops there, close enough to touch it, with the lobby dark behind him and nothing between him and her but the wall and the blue.

On the screen they’ve gone to a picture of the map again, with a red dot where the coast bends, and then to a phone held up in a street somewhere in the dark, people moving through the frame too fast to see. Lena watches it with her chin on her knees. Then something makes her turn her head, the movement or the cold off the glass or nothing, and she sees him.
She looks at him through the wall. He can’t tell how long. Long enough that he knows he should do something with his hands and doesn’t.

She reaches down the couch for the remote. She points it at the set, the way she’d point at a man across a room to say *you*, and the picture goes, and the blue goes with it, and the Fishbowl is a glass box in the dark with a girl in it.

She doesn’t get up. She sits on in the dark, with her knees up and the remote in her hand, and the only light on her now is the red of the exit sign over the front doors, a little of it, along one cheek.
It’s for him. He knows that much.

choices.key: At three in the morning you saw Lena alone in the Fishbowl and kept walking.
response: He keeps walking, past the glass and the blue and the back of her head, to the basement door, and goes down.

Down there the washers are dark and the floor is dry again and the room still smells of the storm, and the Coke machine takes his four quarters and thinks about it, and drops two cans into the tray, one after the other, *clunk, clunk*. He stands there with one in each hand. It’s the first thing that has gone his way since Saturday, and there’s nobody to tell.

When he comes back up the Fishbowl is dark. The set is off. The couch is empty, the cushion she was on still pressed down at one end, and the remote is lying on the arm of the couch, squared to the edge of it, exactly, the way she lines up a pencil with a book.
He stands at the glass with a Coke in each hand going cold against his palms.

s10b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:16 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: Inside the glass it’s warmer, and close, and quiet: the hum the set makes with the sound off, the rain on the window behind the couches. He sits down at the far end of her couch, on the arm side, with the Carhartt still zipped. She doesn’t look away from the screen.
“Six-point-one,” she says. “They’re saying.”

It’s morning there. The light in the footage is gray and new, and it comes from somebody’s phone, held up and shaking, in a street in Port-au-Prince where people have been sleeping out in the road since last Tuesday because there’s nothing left to sleep in. They come up off the road all at once. A woman in a nightgown with a little boy on her hip runs straight into the middle of the street, away from a wall; a man goes down on his knees in the dust with both hands up, and stays there; a girl in a school sweater is screaming a name nobody in this room will ever know. On one side of the street there are no buildings at all anymore, only a long slope of broken concrete with rebar coming out of it like weeds, and as the phone swings across it the dust comes up off it a second time. Then the picture jerks and drops and is somebody’s feet running, and then a man in a studio again, with a map.
She watches all of it with her knees up and her arms around them and her phone shut in the hollow of her lap.

He watches it too. It’s what there is to do with his eyes. He knows where she is on the couch without looking the way he knows where the stove is in Nonna’s kitchen in the dark: the gray cardigan, a T-shirt under it, her hair still damp at the ends and twisted up in a knot with a pencil pushed through it, out of habit, with nothing to write on. Her feet are bare, tucked under the hem of the cardigan, and one ankle shows, and he looks at the map. It’s the first time since the back hall at Sully’s that he’s been in a room with her and nobody else, and the room is a glass box in a dark lobby at three in the morning, and nothing is happening in it but the end of the world somewhere else.

The rain gets heavier on the window and eases off. On the screen they show the street again from the start, and then a reporter in a flak vest standing in front of a tent city in the dark, and then the map with the red dot. Under her breath, so low it’s mostly the shape of it, she’s praying. He catches enough of it, once, when the set goes quiet between segments — *never was it known* — to know which one.

He has his own. He says a Hail Mary at the woman in the nightgown, and another at the man on his knees in the road, with his mouth shut, the way Nonna taught him for sirens: fast, no frills, like a man throwing a rope. Two prayers going up out of one glass box in a dark lobby, a couch apart, and neither of them for each other.
Her eyes don’t come off the screen.
“You don’t have to sit with me.”
“I know.”

He stays. He sits there with his hands between his knees and watches the people in Haiti come up out of the street over and over, and every few minutes the red band along the bottom crawls the same sentence past, and the man with the map points to the same place on the coast. The couch is the length it is.

The cable box under the set says 3:31 when she puts her feet down. She stands, and pulls the cardigan closed across her front with both hands and holds it there, and goes to the glass door, and gets it open, and turns around with her hand still on it.
“Whatever you’re doing, Jack — you can stop.”
“Doing what?”
Her hand finds the door frame, and holds it, and lets go.

He’s alone in the glass box with the set. He goes back over the week looking for it. He’s taken the last pew. He’s sat at the dryer end of the basement with his back to the room. He looked away first. He’s kept out of every room she was in that he could keep out of, and the rooms he couldn’t, he’s kept to the far end of. He’s been keeping out of her way. If there’s a harder way to keep out of somebody’s way, he doesn’t know it. He doesn’t know what else she could mean.

On the screen the phone comes up in the gray street again, shaking, and the woman in the nightgown runs out into the middle of the road with the little boy on her hip, from the same doorway, the same way, the boy’s arm around her neck, and the dust comes up behind them off the broken concrete again.

s10a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL, THE 3RD–4TH LANDING
body: Rain is coming down the landing window in ropes, so the lamps on the walk below are only smears of yellow, and the glass hums in its frame every time the wind leans on that side of the building. He doesn’t open it. He sits on the third step from the top with his back against the cinderblock, which is cold through the Carhartt.

body.text: *You can stop.* It goes around in him with the rain, in her voice, with her hand on the door frame, and it doesn’t get any clearer for going around.
Behind his eyes the Fishbowl is still a box of dark in the dark lobby, and the red of the exit sign along one side of her face, and the remote in her hand.
The two Cokes are on the step beside him, unopened, sweating onto the concrete. He keeps seeing the remote on the arm of the couch, lined up with the edge.

body: His own pack has been in the inside pocket of the Carhartt since Saturday, against his ribs, with the lighter. In the other pocket, the tin, which isn’t his: eleven.

body.text: Saturday’s, on the church steps, was the first since New Year’s.
He hasn’t lit one since Christmas.

body: It isn’t like wanting a drink of water. It’s lower down and meaner than that, in the hands first, then the chest, an itch with an opinion; it came up the stairs behind him from the lobby, and it has been sitting on the step beside him since. Upstairs, through the fire door, somebody’s alarm clock goes off for no reason and gets slapped quiet. The building ticks with water in its gutters.
His hand is already inside the jacket. He can feel the cellophane under his fingers, the corner of the pack, the lighter warm from him.

response: He goes up the last flight to the roof door and pushes it open on the night and props it with the toe of his sneaker. The rain comes in at once, onto his knees and the top step. He sits in the gap with the door against his foot and lights one of his own with his back to the wind, and smokes it in the noise of the roof, the water coming off the parapet in sheets a few yards away, and doesn’t taste it much.
When it’s down to the filter he pinches it out wet and puts the end in his pocket. His jeans are soaked to the thigh.

He pushes the pack back down into the inside pocket, below the lighter, and zips the Carhartt to the throat over it. Then he sits on the step with his hands outside the jacket, one on each knee, and keeps them there, and listens to the rain do what it’s doing to the window until the hum in the glass is just a sound again.
He takes the tin out of the other pocket instead and opens it on his knee, under the bad light. RELIQUARY on the lid. He counts them with one finger. Each one is a place.
Eleven.
He shuts it. The lid makes its small flat sound, and he holds the tin closed in his hand a while before it goes back.

s14.slug: THURSDAY · 12:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PAGES, AND A HYPOTHETICAL
body: The rain on the window toward the Grove has gone steady and close, and under it, from Theo’s side of the room, comes Theo’s breathing, which is too even and too quiet to be a man asleep. Jack has the desk lamp bent down low over the legal pad so the light stays on his side of the divider. Hollis is on Theo’s nightstand in the teacup, catching a little of the lamp.

Three pages on why you are wrong. He has a page and a half, and an eraser worn down to the metal, and Theo’s blazer on the back of his own chair where Theo threw it at ten past eleven, because Theo’s chair has Hollis’s salad bowl on it. *Frankenstein* is open face down on the desk to the trial, the spine cracked white at the page where Victor says the tortures of the accused didn’t equal his. Jack has underlined that one so many times since last Thursday the paper’s gone soft.

body.text: Hale gave him the wrong side and the wrong side is winning. He spent Thursday telling the table Victor was right to keep his mouth shut, and now he’s up past midnight arguing against silence, against himself, and every sentence he writes for it is better than anything he said at the table last week.

He gave Lena the point on Thursday, and Hale made him take it back in writing: three pages defending Victor’s silence against his own conscience. Every sentence comes out sounding like a lawyer for somebody he doesn’t like.

He’s writing about the priest — Justine’s confessor, who frightened a girl into a lie and called it absolution. *Mr. Costigan may include the clergy.* He has. He keeps having to stop and take the adjectives out.

He’s arguing against silence, the way she argued it on Thursday, from her end of the table, and it goes easier than it should. He keeps writing sentences she could have said, and having to cross them out because she did.
The Giorgio’s placemat is taped to the top of page one, grease spot and all, with Calabria showing through from the back.

The placemat is folded in four in the Carhartt on the back of his chair, where he put it. He copied the one sentence out at the top of page one in his own hand, and he’s trying to write the rest like it.

body: He writes a sentence. He erases it. He writes it again, worse, and leaves it.
“How many pages,” Theo says from the dark, not a question.
“A page and a half.”

“Hale will smell it on you. He can smell a page and a half from the stairs. He once failed a Rhodes Scholar for a paragraph that was *trying*; I read it somewhere reputable.” The sheets go. “Hollis has a pledge breakfast at six-thirty and a chapter dinner at seven, and at midnight he is either a brother or an omelet, and I’d like to be awake for whichever.”
“You’ve been awake since Monday.”
“I’ve been awake since puberty,” Theo says. “Write your page and a half.”
Jack writes. Theo goes quiet over there, and the quiet goes on long enough that Jack has nearly finished a paragraph inside it.
The next thing out of the dark is a pitch.

“Hypothetically. I’m developing something. A man has a friend — a girl. Her boyfriend from home ends it. The man stays put. He has his own girl. He’s decent about it. A week later the friend is with a musician.”
Jack’s pencil has stopped. He doesn’t turn around. On the nightstand the egg sits in its cup.
“Question for the room,” Theo says. “Is the man hurt, or relieved?”
“That’s a terrible pitch.”
The bedsprings go as Theo turns over, toward him, toward the lamp. He doesn’t sit up.
“A week, Costigan.”

It lands somewhere under his ribs and sits there. He knows who the man is; Theo might as well have put up a photograph. Wes, on All Souls. Julian by the middle of the month — she told him in the Grove, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs. He isn’t going to talk about any of that to the dark at midnight.
What he doesn’t know is why Theo Vance, who falls asleep when he decides to, is lying awake past midnight in the dark with an egg on his nightstand and a pitch he’s said twice.

choices.text: “Hurt. He’d be hurt. He’d tell everybody he wasn’t.”
choices.key: At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You told him the man would be hurt.
response: “Hurt,” Jack says, to the legal pad. “He’d be hurt. He’d tell everybody he wasn’t.”
Nothing comes back out of the dark for so long that he thinks Theo has finally gone under.
“Good note,” Theo says, short, and turns back over to the wall.

Jack sits there with the pencil and the thing he just said out loud, for the second time this week, to the second person. It doesn’t get any easier the second time. It gets realer. He bends the lamp lower and goes back to Victor.

He finishes at ten past two. The last page is the easiest, which he doesn’t trust. He writes his name at the top of page one, and the class, and Hale’s name, and stops with the pencil on the line where the date goes.

choices.text: “The man should get a roommate who sleeps.”
choices.key: At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You told him to get the man a roommate who sleeps.
response: “The man,” Jack says, “should get a roommate who sleeps.”
“The roommate has insomnia.” Theo settles back into his pillow, unbothered. “It’s a character trait. It gives him texture. Audiences respond to it.”
“Go to sleep, Theo.”

“I’m in development,” Theo says, and is quiet, and the quiet doesn’t sound like sleep either. Jack can feel him over there in the dark, waiting for a better answer, and he doesn’t give him one. He bends the lamp lower and goes back to Victor in the courtroom.

At ten past two Jack writes the last sentence of page three and doesn’t read it over. He turns back to page one and writes his name at the top, and the class, and stops on the line for the date with the pencil resting there, and can’t think, for the life of him, what it is.

choices.text: *Pretend to be asleep at the desk.*
choices.key: At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You pretended to be asleep at your desk.
response: He puts his forehead down on his arm on the legal pad, and breathes slow, and lets the pencil roll out of his fingers to the edge of the desk.
From the dark, after a while: “You don’t erase in your sleep, Costigan.”

He doesn’t lift his head. Theo doesn’t say anything else. After a minute Jack hears him turn over toward the wall, and after another he sits up and picks up the pencil off the edge of the desk where it stopped, and erases, and goes on.

By ten past two he has three pages, and he gets them in order with the lamp bent low, and writes his name at the top of the first one and the class under it, and stops with the pencil on the space where the date goes and leaves it blank.

body: The storm comes into Hollis 302 as light. At the window end the glass is running white and bright and the eucalyptus outside is thrashing in it, so the long table looks wet at that end; at the door end, under the clock, there’s only the overhead fluorescent and the radiator.

He has been in the third-floor stairwell since ten to one, with his pages in a folder under his arm and the RAZR open in his hand to the clock. The stairwell window looks down on the Hollis steps, and from it he watched Julian walk her across from the Commons under a black umbrella, held over her and not over himself, so the rain went down his own back the whole way. At the door Julian’s hand was at the small of her back, and she went in.

He comes in a minute before Hale. Evan is at the door with the roster on a clipboard, taking pages and checking names, and Jack hands his over and Evan checks him off without looking up. She’s at the window end, the last chair, with her back to the glass; her pages are already on the stack, and her *Frankenstein* is lined up with the table edge and the pencil across it. He takes the door end, under the clock. Yusuf is in the corner with his coffee.

She didn’t look up when the door opened. Last week she looked up and went back to her page; this week the page is enough. The radiator knocks under the window. He gets his own copy out and opens it to the trial, and the margins he wrote in October look like somebody else’s handwriting, a boy with opinions.
Caleb has his phone out under the table edge, turned toward Yusuf, and he says it at the volume of a man who thinks he’s being discreet. “Costigan’s on TwitPic. Constitutional law in a monsoon.”
Yusuf looks at the phone and then at his coffee. Jack sees the back of it, Caleb’s thumb on the screen, and not the picture.
At the window end Lena turns a page.
Hale comes in with the rain on his shoulders and takes the stack from Evan, and the roster with it, and sits down halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end.

“Three pages each on why you are wrong,” he says. “I have read every first sentence on the stairs, which is as far as most editors go and further than most readers. Most of you have written three pages on why you are right, with a paragraph at the end in which you are briefly and decoratively wrong. That is not an argument. That is a fucking curtsy.” He lifts the stack and lets it drop on the table. “I shall now read you one sentence from each, of my choosing, which you will find instructive or humiliating, and I don’t mind which.”

Every time Hale reads a name that isn’t his or hers, Lena writes something in her margin, small, with the pencil out of her hair; every time he turns a page, Jack’s eyes go to the window end and come back to the table before they get there. It’s like keeping your hand out of a pocket. He has had a lot of practice at that this week.

He goes down the roster in no order Jack can see. He reads Caleb’s — *Victor’s fear of being thought mad is the only sane thing about him* — and says, “Hargrove, no,” and goes on. He reads a girl from the window side on the miniature in Justine’s pocket, and nods. He reads Yusuf’s — *Nobody in Geneva asked the servant what she saw* — and lays it face down without a word, gently.
He runs his finger down Evan’s list.
“Broussard,” Hale reads, in the Oxford voice, off the roster. “Magdalena T.”

It goes into Jack whole. Not her eyes this time, and not the verse — the first chorus, all of it at once, folded into her name in an Englishman’s mouth: the Bastille with the stools pushed back and the room gone quiet for it, Julian with his eyes shut over the guitar, a man outside a door with nothing to get in with but her name, saying it every way he knows, and at the end of it, every time, the name. Hale reads it the way he’d read out a train time.
“Lena, please,” she says, evenly, from the window end.
Hale looks up from the list. “Lena. Forgive me. The registrar is a romantic.”
Caleb laughs, and finds out alone that it isn’t a laughing matter, and turns it into a cough. Evan looks down at his clipboard as if the registrar might be on it.
In the garden she doesn’t know him until he says her name, and then she answers. Here she answers with a name that isn’t in the song.
Hale finds her page in the stack and reads it out.

body.title: From Lena’s pages, read aloud
body.text: *There is a silence that isn’t cowardice: when the truth would only be one more thing taken from people who have already lost everything.*

body: Her hand goes up to the medal at her collar while he reads, and takes hold of it through the cardigan.
Jack sees the hand.
Hale lays the page down and is quiet a moment. “Miss Broussard has defended silence better than Victor ever managed,” he says. “Which is a terrible thing to be able to say about anyone.”

It goes past Jack close, the sentence, like a truck past a man walking the shoulder of 422. There are things he doesn’t think about. He’s good at it. He sits with his hands on the table and doesn’t think about them now, and at the window end her hand doesn’t move from her collar, and her eyes don’t move from Hale.
The rain goes across the window in a gust, and every pen at the table stays down.
“Costigan,” Hale says, and finds his.

body.text: He reads it in the same voice he gave the train time. *A man who keeps quiet to save himself has already confessed; he’s only chosen the wrong confessor.* He looks down the table at the door end. “Mr. Costigan has prosecuted himself and won. Appeal denied.”

He reads it with a little relish, as if it were a menu in bad French. *Victor was right to keep quiet, and I do not believe a word of this paragraph.* He sets it down. “The most honest sentence in the stack, and it’s a lie. Well done.”

*A confessor who frightens a girl into a lie has stopped hearing confessions and started taking them.* Hale reads it twice over in his head, by the look of him, before he says anything. “He has included the clergy.”

*Victor’s silence isn’t the sin; the sin is the year he spent making it sound like a reason.* Hale reads it without any voice on it at all, and looks down the table at him a moment. “Better. Late, but better.”

body: It’s strange to hear it read, his own sentence in that voice, in that room, with the rain going across the window behind her. It sounds smaller than it did at two in the morning. It sounds truer. Down the table Lena hasn’t looked at him; she’s looking at the page in Hale’s hand.
Then Hale turns his head toward the door end and leaves it there.

body.text: “You have both defended him, Mr. Costigan. She did it better, and meant it less. Answer her.”
“You went after the clergy, Mr. Costigan. Miss Broussard has gone after you. Answer her.”
“Mr. Costigan. She has made your Thursday case against you, and made it better. Answer her.”

body: The table turns with him, one face at a time: Caleb, the window girls, Evan with his pen up, Yusuf over his coffee lid. At the window end her hand is still at her collar. She’s looking at Hale, and only at Hale, and the storm light is all down one side of her.

journal.title: The medal
journal.text: Lena’s medal was her grandmother’s; it came back to her mother in a plastic bag. When she’s working something out, her hand goes to it. At the Point in December. Thursday at Hale’s table, about Justine. Saturday in the hall at Sully’s, about the Fishbowl. Thursday at Hale’s table, while he read out her paper about keeping quiet.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning she was in the Fishbowl with the news. I kept walking. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena.

choices.key: At Hale’s table you said Lena was right. She usually is.
response: “She’s right,” Jack says. “She usually is.”
It’s true, and he lets it stand. At the window end Lena’s pencil stops on the page.

Hale looks at him, and down the table at her, and back, and picks up the next page off the stack without a remark. The hour goes on without either of them in it. Caleb argues for madness for twenty minutes and loses.

When the chairs go back she’s the first one up. She goes out by the far door at the window end, the one nobody uses, with the book flat against her chest, so she never has to come down the table past him.
Her chair is pushed in. Her end of the table is bare, except for the light coming across it off the rain.

choices.text: “Silence that protects the guilty is a second crime.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you argued your page at Hale: silence that protects the guilty is a second crime.
response: He says it to Hale, not to the window end. “Silence that protects the guilty is a second crime.”
Hale sits back in his chair as if somebody has finally poured him a drink. “*There* he is.”

“Go on,” says Hale, and he goes on — Victor in the courtroom with the proof sitting in his own chair, the girl in the cart, every day he let it stand — and he wins it, he can feel the table come over to him a sentence at a time, Caleb nodding, Evan writing fast. At the window end Lena’s hand comes down off the medal to the table and lies there, flat, beside the book.

She says nothing for the rest of the hour. When the chairs go back she’s up first, and out by the far door at the window end with her book against her chest, the door nobody uses, and she doesn’t come down the table to do it.
The chair at the window end is still pushed back from the table, with the storm light on the seat.

choices.key: At Hale’s table you wouldn’t argue it again. You said what you wrote.
response: “I said what I wrote.”
He doesn’t say it again. Saying it again would mean saying it down the table, to her, and he’s had enough of the far end of things for one week.
Hale looks at him down the length of the table. “You wrote it beautifully,” he says. “You didn’t say it.” And he goes on to the next page.
At the window end the hand comes away from her collar, at some point in the next sentence; he doesn’t see when.

When the chairs go back she’s the first one up, and goes out by the far door at the window end with the book held flat against her chest. It’s the long way to the stairs. It keeps her off his end of the table.
In the corner Yusuf puts the lid back on his coffee, pressing it down all the way round with his thumb until it clicks.

choices.text: “Some people are very good at keeping quiet.”
choices.key: At Hale’s table you said some people are very good at keeping quiet. Lena said, ‘Some people are.’
response: “Some people,” Jack says, “are very good at keeping quiet.”
He means the back hall at Sully’s. He means whatever it was she had in her mouth and kept there, with the halftime show coming through the wall.
Her hand is still closed on the medal. She looks down the table at him, the whole length of it, for the first time today.
“Yes,” she says. “Some people are.”
Caleb stops writing. Hale turns over the next page.
He landed it. He can tell he landed it by how still she’s gone, and it doesn’t feel like anything he wanted, and the hour goes on around it.

When the hour is done she is up before anyone and out the far door at the window end, the one nobody uses, without coming past his chair. Under the window the radiator knocks, and goes on knocking at the empty end of the table.

body: The downspout outside 412 has been running since Tuesday, and tonight it has found a rhythm, a long pour and a knock, a long pour and a knock, like somebody patient at a door. Theo is sitting on the edge of his bed in the navy blazer with his phone in his hand, still damp at the shoulders, and the teacup on the nightstand beside him.
“That was Brooks,” he says. “Hollis has made it. Thursday to Thursday. I’m in.” He puts the phone face down on the blanket. “Brooks says I may keep him or eat him.”
“Congratulations, Brother Vance.”
“Please. It makes me sound like I make jam.”
“We should get him a plaque.”

“He’d hate it. He’s a very private egg.” Theo is smiling at the cup anyway. “I’m keeping him.” He picks up the cup in both hands and looks at the egg, the HOLLIS in somebody else’s blue ink, a week of stairwells and sandbags and storm and one salad bowl. He sets it back down on the nightstand exactly where it was.

body.text: “Hollis Ashby retires with honors.”
“Hollis retires with honors.”

body: The cup sits on the nightstand in the lamplight, and the egg in it.
Theo looks around the room, at his own bed and the closet and the floor. “Costigan. My umbrella.”
“It lost an argument with the Supreme Court.”
“Most of us do,” Theo says, and turns out his lamp.
Jack moves his stapler to plug in the RAZR, and there’s a yellow Post-it under it, half-tucked, in Theo’s hand.

body.title: A Post-it, under the stapler
body.text: COMMUNICATION IS THE BEDROCK OF —

body: He holds it up to the desk lamp.
“That’s not for you,” Theo says, from the dark.
Jack puts it back under the stapler. He turns off the lamp and gets into bed, and the room goes to the streetlamp under the blind and the rain.
After a while, from the other bed, short:
“Over Christmas. You called her every night.”
Jack looks at the ceiling.
“Most nights.”
“Most nights,” Theo says, slowly, as if he’s writing it down.

He doesn’t say anything else, and Jack doesn’t ask him why he wants to know. It’s there in the room anyway, once it’s said: the garage on Glenwood Avenue with the door down, the cold coming up out of the concrete through his socks, the space heater ticking, the phone hot against his ear, and her voice coming up the line from Louisiana, an hour at a time.
The RAZR buzzes on his chest.

home. the swing hooks are just hanging there now. like earrings. tomorrow you owe me conan

body: He holds the phone up over his face and reads it, and the little screen lights his hand and a square of the ceiling, and the cold garage goes wherever it goes. Tomorrow. Conan’s last night, and her house, and the popcorn, and her crying about a man she’s never met.
He types it with his thumb.

body.text: conan. your house. im bringing pop

body: He closes the phone and lets it lie on his chest, and it goes up and down there with his breathing, and across the room Theo’s breathing has gone slow at last, for real, and outside the window the downspout pours, and knocks, and pours.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg.
